query: 2026 Tour de France Stage 19 Gap to Alpe d'Huez July 24 - profile, favorites, and any preview analysis. Historical base rate of how often Alpe d'Huez summit finishes are won by breakaway vs GC favorites vs Pogačar specifically.
answer:
Report submitted. Key takeaways for the forecasting caller:

**Stage profile:** 127.9 km, ~3,500 m climbing, Gap → Alpe d'Huez. Two hard climbs in the first 25 km (Col Bayard, Col du Noyer) designed to shape the break, then ~65 km of valley, then Col d'Ornon and the 13.8 km / 8.1% summit finish.

**Outcome:** Pogačar won in yellow, attacking the GC group ~12 km out and bridging a 3:30 gap to a 42-rider break, setting a record 35:26 ascent (−1:14 on Pantani's 36:40).

**Base rates** — the core deliverable, from a hand-classified table of all 33 Alpe d'Huez summit finishes:

| Window | Breakaway | GC group |
|---|---|---|
| All-time (32 mass-start) | 28% (9) | 72% (23) |
| 2001–2022 (pre-2026 view) | 33% (3/9) | 67% (6/9) |
| 2001–2026 | 36% (4/11) | 64% (7/11) |

Pogačar specifically: 1 win from 3 career Alpe d'Huez ascents (2022 5th at +3:23; 2026 S19 win; 2026 S20 domestique duty at +1:05).

Three things worth flagging:

- **A widely-repeated media claim is wrong.** Cyclingnews, intervals.icu and others called 2026 the first back-to-back Alpe d'Huez in Tour history. The 1979 Tour finished there on both stages 17 and 18; Wikipedia's 1979 page says so explicitly. What's actually new in 2026 is the two *different* approach routes.
- **The breakaway/GC dichotomy is genuinely fuzzy here.** 1989 (130 km solo), 2015 (Pinot bridged from the GC group to break remnants) and 2026 S19 itself (Pogačar attacked from the GC group and *caught* the break) resist clean classification. Reclassifying 1989 moves the all-time rate to 25%/75%.
- **Confidence is uneven.** Mechanism classifications for 1981, 1982 and 1983 rest on thinner reporting than the rest and are flagged as such in the table; they move the aggregate by at most ~3 pp.

key_facts: 2026 TdF Stage 19 ran Gap to Alpe d'Huez on Friday 24 July 2026: 127.9 km with ~3,500 m of climbing, starting 14:15 CEST.

Climbs in order: Col Bayard (4.7 km @ 7.2%), Col du Noyer (7.2 km @ 8.5%), Lac du Sautet climb (2.7 km @ 6%), Col d'Ornon (5.4 km @ 6.4%), Alpe d'Huez (13.8 km @ 8.1%, 21 hairpins, finish at 1,850 m).
Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) won the stage in 3:17:57, beating Lenny Martinez by 6 seconds and Richard Carapaz by 9 seconds.

Pogačar attacked from the GC group roughly 11.7-12 km from the summit — no other GC rider followed — bridged a 3:30 deficit to the breakaway survivors, and dropped Carapaz and Martinez with ~800-900 m to go.
Pogačar's ascent time of 35:26-35:27 broke Marco Pantani's 1995 record of 36:40 by 1:14; estimated ~6.9 W/kg overall, 7.1-7.3 W/kg in the opening portion after his attack.
A 42-rider breakaway formed over Col Bayard, reached ~4:30, and had ~3:30-3:35 at the foot of Alpe d'Huez with 14-15 riders left.
Pogačar became only the second rider ever to win at Alpe d'Huez while wearing the yellow jersey, after Geraint Thomas in 2018.

The widely repeated claim that 2026 was the first back-to-back Alpe d'Huez finish in Tour history is FALSE — the 1979 Tour finished at Alpe d'Huez on both stage 17 (Agostinho) and stage 18 (Zoetemelk). What is new in 2026 is that the two ascents used different approach routes.
Across 32 mass-start Tour stage finishes at Alpe d'Huez (excluding the 2004 ITT), 9 were won from a breakaway (~28%) and 23 from the favourites/GC group (~72%).
Modern-era split (2001-2022, the pre-2026 base rate): 3 of 9 mass-start finishes won from a breakaway (33%), 6 from the GC group (67%). Breakaway wins were 2006 F. Schleck, 2013 Riblon, 2022 Pidcock.
Including both 2026 stages, the 2001-2026 split is 4 of 11 breakaway (36%) and 7 of 11 GC group (64%).

Pogačar's career record at Alpe d'Huez: 3 Tour ascents — 5th in 2022 (+3:23, climb time 39:08), 1st in 2026 stage 19, and ~+1:05 in 2026 stage 20 while riding as a domestique for Isaac del Toro. That is 1 win from 3 ascents, or 1 from 2 when racing for himself.

Pre-race, ProCyclingUK ranked Pogačar the top stage favourite ahead of Evenepoel and Seixas, and predicted exactly that podium; it estimated the break needed roughly a five-minute cushion at the foot of the Alpe to survive.
Entering stage 19, Pogačar led Evenepoel by 4:32, Del Toro by 6:51 and Seixas by 7:11. After the stage the gaps were 7:11, 9:42 and 10:06.

Stage 20 the next day (also to Alpe d'Huez, via Croix de Fer, Télégraphe, Galibier and Sarenne) was won by Richard Carapaz from a 14-rider breakaway after Sepp Kuss crashed twice inside the final 10 km.
Pogačar won the 2026 Tour overall by 6:26 over Evenepoel — a record-equalling fifth title — with 5 stage wins (stages 3, 6, 10, 14, 19).
Only 3 of the 29 pre-2026 Alpe d'Huez stage winners went on to win the Tour overall that same year (per Cyclingnews); Pogačar 2026 makes it 4 of 30.
Jean-Paul Vespini's count (2008) found the rider in yellow after the Alpe d'Huez stage went on to win the Tour in 17 of 25 visits (68%).

Sources disagree on Pantani's benchmark time (36:40, 36:50, 36:53 or 37:35) because timers use different start points and measured distances (13.8 km vs 14.5 km). Pogačar's 35:26 is measured over 13.8 km.

The 1978 Alpe d'Huez stage was won on the road by Michel Pollentier, who took yellow and was then expelled for faking his doping sample with a concealed condom of someone else's urine; Hennie Kuiper (2nd on the road, +37 s) was awarded the win.
